The adults are distinguished by the two-jointed trochanters, the connate abdomen, two apical spurs to the front tibiæ, and a pair of saws at the end of the abdomen of the female. The larvæ often resemble lepidopterous larvæ. They have six true legs, and often from twelve to sixteen prolegs, and are rarely covered with a white waxy secretion. Most species are leaf-feeders, issuing from eggs laid in slits cut in leaves by the female saws.
readings.c3s1: A few forms, however, are twig-borers, or inhabit the stems of cereals or other grasses. They pupate in tough parchment-like silken cocoons. About 700 species are known in Europe, and about 500 in North America. Many
readings.c3s2:

¶
'''Tenthredo''' (ten-thrē′dō), ''n.'' [NL. (Linnæus, 1748), < Gr. τενθρηδών (-δον-), a kind of wasp. Cf. ''drone''<sup>2</sup>.] A genus of saw-flies, typical of the family ''Tenthredinidæ'', at first coextensive with the family, but now restricted to certain forms with long setaceous antennæ, in which the third joint is longer than the fourth, and the lanceolate cell of the fore wings has a straight cross-nervure. They are the largest of the saw-flies next to the ''Cimbicinæ''.

'''tenticle†''' (ten′ti-kl), ''n.'' [< ML. *''tenticula'', dim. of ''tenta'', a tent: see ''tent''<sup>1</sup>.] A little tent.

{{smaller block|They were the ''tenticles'' or rather cabins and couches of their soldiers. ''Patten'', Exped. to Scotland (1548). (''Davies''.)}}

'''tentif†''', ''a.'' Same as ''tentive''.

'''tentifly†''', ''adv.'' See ''tentively''.

'''tentiform''' (ten′ti-fôrm), ''a.'' Shaped like a tent; in ''entom.'', noting the mines of certain tineid larvæ, in which one or the other surface of the infested leaf is raised in a tent-like form.

'''tentiginous†''' (ten-tij′i-nus), ''a.'' [< L. ''tentigo'' (''-gin-''), a tension, lust (< ''tendere'', stretch: see ''tend''<sup>1</sup>, ''tent''<sup>3</sup>), + ''-ous''.] 1. Excited to lust.

{{smaller block|Were you ''tentiginous'', ha? . . .
Did her silk's rustling move you?
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Devil is an Ass, ii. 1.}}}}
readings.c3s3:
¶
2. Producing lasciviousness; lascivious.

{{smaller block|Nothing affects the head so much as a ''tentiginous'' humour, repelled and elated to the upper region, found by daily practice to run frequently up into madness.
{{right|''Swift'', Mechanical Operations of the Spirit, ii.}}}}

'''tenting''' (ten′ting), ''a.'' [< ''tent''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ing''<sup>2</sup>.] Having the form of a tent. [Rare and erroneous.]

{{smaller block|Coverlids gold-tinted like the peach . . .
Fell sleek about him in a thousand folds,
Not hiding up an Apollonian curve
Of neck and shoulder, nor the ''tenting'' swerve
Of knee from knee, nor ankles pointing light;
But rather giving them to the filled sight
Officiously.
{{right|''Keats'', Endymion, ii.}}}}

'''tentive†''' (ten′tiv), ''a.'' [< ME. ''tentif'', ''tentyf'', by apheresis from ''attentif'', attentive: see ''attentive''. Cf. ''tent''<sup>4</sup>. Cf. also ''tenty'', a later form of ''tentive''.] Attentive.

{{smaller block|We schulen do so ''tentyf'' besynes fro day to night that . . . sche shal be hool and sound.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Tale of Melibeus (Harl. MS.).}}}}

{{smaller block|Wyth ''tentiue'' lystning eeche wight was setled in harckning.
{{right|''Stanihurst'', Æneid, ii. 1.}}}}

'''tentively†''' (ten′tiv-li), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''tentifly''; < ''tentive'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] Attentively; carefully.

{{smaller block|ȝif ȝe ''tentifly'' take kepe & trewe be to-gadere,
I wol winne our warisun, for i wot where thei are.
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2258.}}}}

{{smaller block|''Tentifly'' she kept hir fader dere.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Clerk's Tale, l. 278.}}}}

'''tentless''' (tent′les), ''a.'' [< ''tent''<sup>4</sup> + ''-less''.] Inattentive; heedless. [Scotch.]

{{smaller block|I'll wander on, with ''tentless'' heed
How never-halting moments speed,
Till fate shall snap the brittle thread.
{{right|''Burns'', To James Smith.}}}}

'''tent-maker''' (tent′mā″kėr), ''n.'' One who makes tents.

{{smaller block|By their occupation they were ''tentmakers.'' Acts xviii. 3.}}

'''tentorial''' (ten-tō′ri-al), ''a.'' [< ''tentorium'' + ''-al.''] Of or pertaining to the tentorium.—'''Tentorial'''

{{RunningHeader|tent-caterpillar|6236|tentorial}}'''tent-caterpillar''' (tent′kat″ėr-pil-ä̤r), ''n.'' A webworm; the larva of either of two North American bombycid moths of the genus ''Clisiocampa'', ''C. americana'' and ''C. sylvatica''. {{smaller|The former is the tent-caterpillar of the orchard and the latter the tent-caterpillar of the forest. ''C. americana'' feeds normally on the wild cherry, but often does great damage by defoliating the apple and pear. The larvæ live gregariously in great tent-like silken webs (whence the name). Compare ''lackey-moth.'' See also cut on preceding page, and cut under ''Clisiocampa.''}} [[File:century v08 p0040 c1f1.png|center|309px]] {{c|Female Moth of Tent-caterpillar (''Clisiocampa americana'').}} '''tent-cloth''' (tent′klôth), ''n.'' Canvas or duck made for tents, awnings, etc. '''tented''' (ten′ted), ''a.'' [< ''tent''1 + ''-ed''2.] '''1.''' Covered or furnished with tents. {{smaller block|They have used
Their dearest action in the ''tented'' field. {{right|''Shak.'', Othello, i. 3. 85.}} Till sad Mecistheus and Alastor bore
His honour'd body to the ''tented'' shore. {{right|''Pope'', Iliad, xiii. 532.}}}} '''2†.''' Of or like a tent (?). {{smaller block|With Reed-like Lance, and with a blunted Blade,
To Championize vnder a ''Tented'' shade. {{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas's Weeks, ii., The Vocation.}}}} '''tenter1''' (ten′tėr), ''n.'' [< ''tent''1 + ''-er''1.] One who lives in a tent. {{smaller block|The pretty girl of our civilization, who pushes into the canvas home of the ''tenters.'' {{right|''Harper's Mag.'', LXXVII. 801.}}}} '''tenter2''' (ten′tėr), ''n.'' [< ME. ''tenture'', ''tentowre'', < OF. ''tenture'', a stretching, hangings, < ML. ''tentura'', a stretcher, tenter, lit. a stretching, spreading (cf. L. ''tensura'', a stretching: see ''tensure''), < ''tendere'', pp. ''tentus'', ''tensus'', stretch: see ''tend''1, and cf. ''tent''1, ''tent''3, and ''tenture''.] '''1.''' A machine or frame used in the manufacture of cloth to stretch out the pieces of stuff, so that they may set or dry evenly and square. {{smaller|Along the upper and lower crosspieces, which can be fixed apart from each other at any required distance, are numerous sharp hooks, called ''tenter-hooks'', on which the selvages of the cloth are hooked. Sykes, for instance, when his dressing-shop was set on fire and burned to the ground, when the cloth was torn from his ''tenters'' and left in shreds on the field, took no steps to discover or punish the miscreants. {{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Shirley, ii.}}}} 2. Same as ''tenter-hook.'' {{smaller block|O how friends' reasons and their freedoms stretch, When power sets his wide ''tenters'' to their sides! {{right|''Chapman'', Byron's Tragedy, v. 1.}}}} 3. One of the little bristles of a fly's foot; a tentacle. {{smaller block|Beset underneath with small bristles or ''tenters.'' {{right|''Dr. Hooke.''}}}} '''On''' or '''upon the tenter''' or '''tenters,''' on the stretch; on the rack; hence, in distress, uneasiness, or suspense. {{smaller block|How, ''upon the tenters?'' indeed, if the whole peece were so stretcht, and very well beaten with a yard of reformation, no doubt it would grow to a goodly breadth. {{right|''Heywood'', Fair Maid of the Exchange (Works, II. 25).}}}} {{smaller block|It was gallantry that suited her own maiden loftiness, ever stretched ''upon the tenters'' of punctilio. {{right|''Goldsmith'', Sequel to A Poetical Scale.}}}} '''tenter'''2 (ten′tėr), ''v.'' [< ''tenter''2, ''n.''] I. ''trans.'' To hang or stretch on or as on tenters. {{smaller block|Easily we may imagine what acerbity of pain must be endured by our Lord in his tender limbs being stretched forth, racked, and ''tentered.'' ''Barrow'', Works, II. xxxii.}} {{smaller block|We fear he will be bankrupt; he does stretch, ''Tenter'' his credit so; embraces all. {{right|''Fletcher'', Beggars' Bush, ii. 3.}}}} II. ''intrans.'' To support or resist the straining of the tenter; bear tentering. {{smaller block|Woollen cloth will ''tenter.'' {{right|''Bacon.''}}}} '''tenter'''3 (ten′tėr), ''n.'' [< ''tent''4, ''v.'', + ''-er''1.] A tender; one who tends or has the care or oversight of something: as, a cattle-''tenter;'' specifically, a person in a factory who tends or watches machinery; often, also, an overseer or foreman in a factory.—'''Drawing tenter''', {{smaller|in ''cotton-spinning'', an operator whose duty it is to supply full cans in place of the emptied ones, and to mend the slivers when they break.}} '''tenter-bar''' (ten′tėr-bär), ''n.'' In ''bleaching calico, dyeing'', etc., a bar provided with a series of tenter-hooks, and used in a tenter for stretching cloth; also, such a bar used for stretching cloth by hand. {{smaller|It is used by engaging the selvage of the cloth upon the hooks and by pulling upon the bar, stretching the material to the desired extent. See ''tenter''2, 1.}} '''tenter-ground''' (ten′tėr-ground), ''n.'' A ground or space for the erection and maintaining of tenters. {{smaller block|I entered Kendal almost in the dark, and could distinguish only a shadow of the castle on a hill, and ''tenter-grounds'' spread far and wide round the town. {{right|''Gray'', To Dr. Wharton, Oct. 18, 1769.}}}} '''tenter-hook''' (ten′tėr-hu̇k), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. ''tenter-hoke''; < ''tenter''2 + ''hook''.] 1. A hook for stretching cloth on a tenter. {{smaller block|Any Hurts whatsoever, received either by Sword, Cane, or Gun Shot, Knife, Saw, or Hatchet, Hammer, Nail, or ''Tenter hook'', Fire, Blast, or Gunpowder, etc. {{right|Quoted in ''Ashton's'' Reign of Queen Anne, II. 106.}}}} 2. Figuratively, anything that painfully strains, racks, or tortures. {{smaller block|Parasites are his [the prodigal's] ''tenter-hooks'', and they stretch him till he bursts. {{right|''Rev. T. Adams'', Works, I. 496.}}}} {{smaller block|Difficulties which stretched his fine genius on the ''tenter-hooks''. {{right|''I. D'Israeli'', Curios. of Lit., II. 379.}}}} 3. In ''her.'', a bearing representing an iron hook with the straight bar pointed at one end, and projecting beyond the bent or angled part at the other, so that it can be driven in by blows of a hammer.—'''On tenter-hooks.''' {{smaller|Same as ''on the tenters'' (which see, under ''tenter''2).}} {{smaller block|I know Dolly 's ''on tenter-hooks'' now. {{right|''Whyte Melville'', White Rose, II. xxviii.}}}} '''tentering-machine''' (ten′tėr-ing-ma-shēn″), ''n.'' In ''weaving'', a machine for stretching fabrics, consisting of a combination of rollers, which may be driven at different speeds, with devices for feeding and delivery. '''tent-fly''' (tent′flī), ''n.'' A piece of canvas stretched across the ridge-pole of a tent, and secured to the ground by ropes along its lower edges. '''tent-guy''' (tent′gī), ''n.'' A rope, additional to the usual tent-ropes, for the better securing of a tent in a storm. A guy usually passes from the top of each upright to the ground at some distance in front and rear. '''tenth''' (tenth), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< ME. ''tenthe'', ''teonthe'', ''tende'', beside ''tethe'', ''tithe'', E. ''tithe'', the form with ''n'' being due to a mixture with the cognate Icel. ''tīundi'' (see ''teind''), and to conformity with ''ten'', < AS. ''teótha'' = OS. ''tehando'' = OFries. ''tegotha'', ''tegetha'', ''tegatha'', ''tianda'', ''tienda'' = D. ''tiende'' = MLG. ''teinde'' = OHG. ''zehanto'', MHG. ''zehente'' (''zende''), G. ''zehnte'' = Icel. ''tīundi'' = Sw. ''tionde'' = Dan. ''tiende'' = Goth. ''taihunda'', tenth; as ''ten'' + ''-th''2. Cf. ''tithe''.] '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Last in order of a series of ten; preceded by nine of the same kind; next in order after that which is ninth: an ordinal numeral.—'''2.''' Being one of ten equal portions or sections.—{{smaller|'''Tenth nerve''', in ''anat.'', the pneumogastric nerve, as that one of the cranial nerves which comes between the ninth (glossopharyngeal) and the eleventh (spinal accessory) in that enumeration which counts twelve of these structures.}} '''II.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' One of ten equal parts into which anything may be divided; a tithe.—'''2.''' In ''early Eng. law'', a tithe of the rents of the year, or of movables, or both, granted or levied by way of tax. {{smaller|When a tenth was the rate fixed for towns and demesnes, that for the counties exclusive of towns and demesnes}} was usually a fifteenth. 3. ''Eccles.'', the tenth part of the annual profit of every living in England, formerly paid to the Pope, but by statute transferred to the crown, and afterward made a part of the fund called ''Queen Anne's bounty.''—4. In ''music'': (''a'') The interval, whether melodic or harmonic, between any tone and a tone one octave and two degrees distant from it; also, a tone distant by such an interval from a given tone; a compound third. (''b'') An organ-stop giving tones a tenth above the normal pitch of the digitals used; a decima, or double tierce. '''tenthdeal†''', ''adv.'' [ME. ''tenthedel''; < ''tenth'' + ''deal''1. Cf.
